title: Japji 38 and the salok, whole
hookLine: the true mint, and air, water and earth
tomorrow: Simran has two minutes and a hundred stories. which one does she pick?

cards: On Simran's keychain is a squashed penny from a fair, pressed flat in one of those hand-cranked machines. She remembers the squeal of the crank, the warm metal in her palm. A coin doesn't become a coin by wishing.
It gets heated, held and struck. Pauri 38 builds a whole mint like that, and it isn't minting money. It's minting the Word.

teach.h: RESTRAINT THE FURNACE, PATIENCE THE GOLDSMITH.
teach.b: Feel your way through the workshop, paraphrased. Restraint is the furnace. Patience is the goldsmith.
Understanding is the anvil, and knowledge the hammer. Awe works the bellows, discipline is the fire, and love is the crucible, where the nectar is poured.

teach.h: IN THE TRUE MINT, THE WORD.
teach.b: In that true mint, the Word is struck. Nobody does it in a hurry; every tool in the room is a virtue, and the pauri says it's the work of those the kind glance falls on.
Then the closing salok steps outside, out into Bebe's garden, where the sprinkler has just come on. Air is the Guru.

teach.h: AIR GURU, WATER FATHER, EARTH MOTHER.
teach.b: Water is the father. Earth is the great mother. Day and night are the two nurses, and the whole world plays in their lap.
Good and bad deeds are read out in the presence of dharma, and by their own actions some come near and some drift far.
And the last lines: those who remembered the Name and finished their hard work have shining faces, Nanak says, and many are freed along with them.
That's what you'd tell a friend tonight: the Japji's last word isn't about one person getting free alone. Bebe reads it, and her voice goes thin. The soil smells like rain.
Simran has now read the whole thing, out loud, beside her grandmother, and neither of them says anything for a while.

how: Sikhs who keep Nitnem end the morning Japji with this salok; some learn its first line, about air, water and earth, by heart.

o: a separate hymn sung only at weddings
the opening verse that starts the Japji
the Japji's last pauri and closing lines

in pauri 38 patience is the goldsmith
restraint the furnace, patience the goldsmith, love the crucible: every tool is a virtue.

games.q: your friend wants to become a calmer person in a weekend, with one big retreat and then done. what does pauri 38 suggest?
o: it's a mint, not a switch: patience, heat and steady work, over and over.
go for it; the pauri says the Word is struck the moment you decide.
skip it; the pauri says the mint is only for saints, not ordinary people.
games.why: every tool in pauri 38's mint is a slow virtue: restraint, patience, understanding, awe, discipline, love. the Word is struck there, not wished into being.

practice: If you have water nearby, take one slow sip and feel the cool of it all the way down. Then notice the air on your skin, and press your palms or feet against the floor.
Air, water, earth: name each one as you feel it, and go round again.

wordCard.voice: Japji 38 and the salok: the true mint where the Word is struck, and the closing lines, air, water and earth, and faces that shine.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a mint, where coins are struck. in pauri 38 it's where the Word is shaped.

carryVoice: Pocket this: faces shining, and many freed alongside them. The whole Japji, read in a garden that smells like rain.
